implementation_notes: Java's coroutine support is kotlinx.coroutines (a library, not the language), which compiles a suspend function into a continuation-passing state machine and provides structured concurrency (coroutineScope), Dispatchers, Flow, and the ContinuationInterceptor underlying the whole thing. A suspend function that calls another suspend function must itself be suspend - the function colouring - which is why the library provides withContext(Dispatchers.IO) to run a suspending block on the right dispatcher. Java 21's virtual threads are the alternative model: stackful continuations on the JVM, so an ordinary blocking method works and no colouring is needed, at the cost of pinning a carrier thread on a monitor or a native call. The choice is real: kotlinx.coroutines for structured, cancellable, single-threaded-friendly code; virtual threads when you want to keep plain blocking code.
idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines suspend functions (CPS state machine) with coroutineScope/Dispatchers; or Java 21 virtual threads (stackful)
pitfalls: runBlocking blocks a thread and must not be used on a server or UI thread - it exists for main() and tests.
Blocking a Dispatchers.IO thread or pinning a virtual thread (a synchronized block or native call) occupies a carrier and can starve the pool under load.
Catching CancellationException broadly swallows cancellation and breaks structured concurrency - rethrow it.
kotlinx.coroutines' suspend requires the caller to be suspend (function colouring); work around it with withContext, not by blocking.
A coroutine launched into GlobalScope outlives its request and leaks - always use a scope.
